articles.title: Colour modes: what colour a finish paints
articles.summary: A zone can keep your own paint colour, paint one solid colour, paint a gradient, or let the finish bring its own colour. Choosing the mode is the first decision for any zone.
articles.what: BASE COLOR is the dropdown that decides where a finish gets its colour. Use source paint keeps the car's own colour and changes only the shine, which is perfect for gloss, matte, satin, pearl or candy over an existing livery. Solid paints the whole zone one colour. Gradient blends 2 to 10 colours across the whole flat sheet in a direction. Finish colour lets chrome, carbon, holographic and similar finishes bring their own.
when: You are not sure whether to repaint or only change the shine.
A finish changed the colour of your livery and you did not want that.
how: Open the zone and look at BASE COLOR.
Pick Use source paint when the colours must stay and only the shine changes.
Pick a solid colour when the zone should be one new colour.
Pick the custom gradient for a fade, then add the stops.
Leave it on the finish's own colour when you want the chrome or carbon look itself.

controls.effect: One flat colour for the whole zone.

controls.effect: A fade across the flat sheet in a direction.

pitfalls: A finish that brings its own colour replaces your colour. Use a coating base with source paint instead.

deep.body: BASE COLOR decides it. Use source paint keeps the car's own colour and changes only the shine: perfect for gloss, matte, satin, pearl or candy over an existing livery. Solid paints the whole zone one colour. Gradient blends 2 to 10 colours in a direction. Finish colour lets chrome, carbon, holographic and similar finishes bring their own.

deep.heading: Gradients run across the whole sheet
deep.body: A gradient runs across the entire flat sheet, so a horizontal fade follows the sheet columns, not the length of the car. Panels do not line up. Give each panel its own zone if you want a fade per panel.

deep.heading: Colour replacement warning
deep.body: A finish that brings its own colour replaces your colour. If you want to keep your colours, use a coating base with source paint instead.

faq.a: Use source paint.

faq.q: How many colours can a gradient have?
faq.a: 2 to 10 stops.

faq.q: Why does my fade not line up on the bumper?
faq.a: A gradient covers the flat sheet, not the 3D car. Use one zone per panel.

faq.q: Why did chrome replace my colour?
faq.a: A finish with its own colour replaces yours. Use a Foundation finish with source paint.

mistakes.fix: Undo and use a coating or Foundation base with Use source paint.

mistakes.fix: Use a zone per side or panel.

articles.title: Strengths and adjustments on a zone
articles.summary: Four groups of sliders tune a zone: how strong it is overall, how much of the finish replaces your paint, how shiny or metal the spec is, and the colour tweaks hue, saturation and brightness.
articles.what: Intensity is the percentage badge on the zone card, 10 to 100 in steps of 10; presets and Rand set it and there is no slider for it. Base Strength runs 0 to 100 percent in steps of 5: 100 replaces your paint fully and lower values let more of the original show. Spec Strength runs 0 to 100 percent in steps of 5 and scales the shine map. Hue (-180 to 180), Saturation (-100 to 100) and Brightness (-100 to 200) tweak the base colour. Scale and Rotation change the size and angle of the finish's own texture. The three spec sliders push metal, roughness and clearcoat up or down for the whole zone.
when: A finish is too strong, too weak, too coarse or the wrong tint.
You want to nudge a finish instead of hunting for another one.
how: Open the zone and change one slider at a time.
For a weaker look lower Base Strength; for a shinier or flatter look use Spec Strength and the three spec sliders.
For colour, use Hue, Saturation and Brightness.
For size, use Base Scale (0.05 to 5, 1.00 is normal).
Judge it in Render, since fine detail does not show well in the small preview.

deep.body: Intensity is the percentage badge on the zone card, 10 to 100 in steps of 10; presets and Rand set it and there is no slider for it. Spec Strength runs 0 to 100 percent in steps of 5 and scales the shine map. Hue is -180 to 180, Saturation -100 to 100 and Brightness -100 to 200. Base Scale is 0.05 to 5 where 1.00 is normal. Scale and Rotation change the size and angle of the finish's own texture.

deep.heading: Size is not strength
deep.body: When someone says "crushed down to 50 percent" they mean texture scale, not strength. Changing strength when you meant size makes the finish weaker, not smaller.

deep.body: They push metal, roughness and clearcoat up or down for the whole zone. Large moves can cancel the finish: pick a better finish instead.

faq.q: What is the difference between Intensity and Base Strength?
faq.a: Intensity is a percentage badge on the zone card (10 to 100) with no slider of its own. Base Strength is how much of the finish replaces your paint (0 to 100%, step 5).

faq.q: What does Base Scale 1.00 mean?
faq.a: Normal size. Lower is finer, higher is larger (0.05 to 5).

faq.a: No, they are the same number.

articles.title: Steer a finish's colour with hue, saturation and brightness
articles.summary: Most finishes that bring their own palette can be steered with Hue, Saturation and Brightness on the zone, so you do not need to search for a different finish.
articles.what: If a finish is almost right, move the three colour sliders instead of changing finish. Too dark or navy: Brightness up 30 to 40. Leaning violet: Hue down about 15 toward sky blue. Grey looking tinted: Saturation down about 10. Flecks gone grey after darkening: Saturation up. One worked example took a blue-white glow finish with Brightness plus 35, Hue minus 15 and Saturation minus 10 to a light ice blue and steel grey with no gradient.
when: A finish is nearly right but the colour is off.
You want a two-colour look without a gradient.
how: Open the zone with the finish.
Move Brightness first, then Hue, then Saturation, a little at a time.
Check the preview after each move, then Render for the real result.
If you cannot get there, try another finish and tune that one.

deep.heading: Order matters a little
deep.body: Move Brightness first, then Hue, then Saturation, a little at a time, and check the preview after each move. Hue rotates every colour in the finish, not just one.

articles.title: Gradients, and a touch of colour in black
articles.summary: A gradient is laid over the whole flat sheet, so it will not line up from panel to panel. For a little colour coming into black, use a coloured flake or sparkle finish instead of a fade.
articles.what: Because the car is unwrapped, one fade does not continue from the side onto the bumper or the other side, and buyers notice. Use a gradient only for a deliberate whole-sheet effect, or give each panel its own zone and its own fade. A touch of colour in a dark area means sparkles or flecks of that colour, not a gradient. A deep-space flake finish does this: black with blue, purple and silver flake, steered to blue with Brightness about minus 45, Hue about minus 20 and Saturation about plus 60, gave roughly 55 percent pure black with blue flecks. Paint patterns cannot take a colour, so they do not do this job.
when: You want blue in the black without a fade.
A gradient does not line up across the car.
how: For a fade, use one zone per panel and give each its own gradient.
For colour in black, choose a flake finish whose flecks are already the colour you want.
Steer it with Brightness, Hue and Saturation on the zone.
Add a spec pattern on top for texture without changing the colour.
Check the result in Render at full size.

pitfalls: Patterns with strong opacity flood the area with the colour instead of sparkling.

deep.heading: A touch of colour in black
deep.body: Use sparkles or flecks of that colour, not a gradient. A deep-space flake finish (black with blue, purple and silver flake) steered with Brightness about minus 45, Hue about minus 20 and Saturation about plus 60 gave roughly 55 percent pure black with blue flecks.

deep.heading: Patterns cannot do this job

articles.title: What common buyer words mean in the app
articles.summary: Everyday words such as crushed down to 50 percent, a touch of colour, the same shade and keep the strokes each have a precise meaning in the app: scale, sparkles, a sampled colour and a fill-only recolour.
articles.what: People describe changes in everyday words, and a few of them have a precise meaning here. Pattern size or crushed down means the zone's texture scale (0.05 to 5) and the spec pattern scale, not spec strength or overall intensity. A touch of colour in a dark area means flecks, not a fade. Only the yellow in the logo means pick that colour, with a tolerance, on that art's layer inside a small box. Same shade means sample the colour from the car instead of guessing a name. Keep the strokes means recolour only the fill colour with a tight tolerance and leave the outline colours alone. Starting from the base file means clean zones: reset them rather than undoing many steps.
when: You are describing a change to the helper or to support.
A reply changed the wrong thing.
how: For size use Base Scale or the pattern Scale; leave strength alone unless you mean strength.
For a colour from the car use PICK COLOR FROM CAR.
To recolour only a fill, keep Tolerance low.
To begin from the base file, use Reset All Zones.

articles.title: Recolour only part of a piece of art
articles.summary: To change just a number fill or one colour in a logo, make a zone limited to that art's layer, pick the exact fill colour and keep the tolerance tight so the outline survives.
articles.what: Use a zone limited to the Numbers layer and the fill colour. Sample the real fill first: dark fills are often close to a black outline, so keep the tolerance around 10 to 16. For a colour inside one logo, combine the colour with a small box around the logo and limit the layers to the decal layers. Without the layer limit the box also grabs body paint whose original colour matches. Then zoom the preview to confirm the outline and drop stroke survived.
when: You want a different number fill but the same outline.
You want to recolour one colour of a logo.
how: Add a zone and use PICK COLOR FROM CAR on the fill colour.
Tick only the art's layer under RESTRICT TO LAYERS.
Keep the tolerance low (about 10 to 16), and draw a small box around a logo if needed.
Choose the new colour and finish, then zoom the preview to check the outline.

articles.title: Start of every design session
articles.summary: Turn the template layers Wire, Mask and Car Mandatory off before judging the preview, read the zones, and make sure only one Shokker page is open.
articles.what: Template layers can be on by default to show the panels, and they draw grids, outlines and fake headlights over the preview you are judging. With Mask off, the empty space between panels shows the base colour: that is not on the car, and iRacing never shows it. Zone numbers move when zones are added on top, so read the zone list before editing and use names. If two different designs show on consecutive reads, two Shokker pages are open: close the other one first.
when: You start a new design on a layered template.
The preview shows grids or outlines.
how: Look at the layer list (right column) and switch off Wire, Mask and Car Mandatory (the group named Turn Off Before Exporting).
Read the zone list top to bottom before adding or changing anything.
Close any second Shokker window or tab.
Then make your changes and check each one in the preview.
tips: The template layers are for placing things; they are off for the final.
pitfalls: The empty space between panels is not part of the car, whatever colour it shows.

articles.title: Effects the preview cannot show
articles.summary: The live preview is much smaller than the real 2048 paint, so fine sparkle, micro-flake and small-scale patterns average out. Candy, chrome and metal twists show in the spec views and in Render.
articles.what: Do not conclude a finish did nothing from the small picture. Zoom a crop, read the spec views, or Render. In the spec views red is metal, green is roughness and blue is clearcoat, where high means dull. In one test a holographic drift finish at a small scale looked flat green in the spec view, yet measured clearly metal against plain gloss. Candy, chrome and metal twists are invisible in the flat colour preview, so confirm them on the spec views.
when: A fine effect seems to have done nothing.
You are judging sparkle or holographic shimmer.
how: Open the spec views and look at R METAL, G ROUGH and B COAT.
Zoom into a crop of the preview.
Render and judge at full size.
Compare with the plain gloss version of the same zone if unsure.
tips: The spec views tell you what iRacing will light, even when the colour picture looks the same.
pitfalls: Do not remove a finish because the small picture looks flat.

articles.title: Things that went wrong before: avoid them
articles.summary: Do not undo many steps after resetting by hand, do not expect lightning on matte black to read as bolts, and remember the empty space between panels keeps the old colour.
articles.what: These are lessons from real sessions. Undoing many steps after you reset zones by hand can bring back an old state with dozens of zones; mute or edit back instead, or reset. The lightning paint pattern on matte black reads as grey cracked glass, not bolts, at any scale. The base colour of a scheme is limited to the paintable area, so once Mask is hidden, the empty space keeps the old colour; that is harmless in iRacing. The zone list does not show scale or spec strength, so if you set a value by hand keep it in mind before a helper overwrites it. On some cars a part such as the spoiler has no body paint pixels, so schemes skip it.
when: Something odd came back after an undo.
A pattern looks wrong on black.
how: To go back, mute the zone or edit it back instead of many undo steps.
To start clean, press Reset All Zones.
Try a different pattern on matte black than lightning.
Check the car's parts article if a part seems to be skipped.
pitfalls: Many undo steps after a manual reset can bring back an older state.

articles.title: Make artwork appear when light hits it
articles.summary: Use two spec-only zones on the art with your picture left unchanged: matte on the whole art layer, then satin chrome on the art's light tones above it. The shape then flashes silver as the light sweeps.
articles.what: The picture never changes, only the shine map. The whole art layer gets a soft matte base so shadows absorb light. Above it, a second zone takes only the art's light tones (colours such as light grey, with a tolerance near 40) and gets a satin chrome. In the sim the light parts flash silver as the sun or track lights sweep, and the dark parts stay dead, so the shape appears out of the paint. Check the spec view: chrome should sit only on highlights, matte on shadows.
when: You want a face, mask or logo to light up on the track.
You want a hidden image that shows only in the light.
how: Add a zone limited to the art layer with a Matte foundation finish and BASE COLOR on your own paint.
Add a second zone above it, same layer, picking the light tones with a tolerance around 40, with a satin chrome foundation finish.

articles.title: Change only the shine and keep the paint exactly
articles.summary: Use a Foundation finish with the base colour set to source paint. It changes the shine map and leaves the colour exactly as it is; ordinary chrome, metallic or candy bases repaint the car.
articles.what: Spec-only looks are the safest way to change shine on a finished livery. Foundation finishes (the ones named Foundation or starting with f) are made to do this. On real templates the paint changed 0 percent with Foundation finishes, and about 78 to 85 percent of a hood changed with ordinary chrome, metallic or candy. Looks: mirror chrome, satin chrome, dark chrome, polished metal, matte metal, pearl, satin pearl, candy, brushed metal, frosted, matte, satin and gloss. A finish that brings its own pattern can also be given a solid colour: you then keep the colour flat and get only its texture in the shine map.

articles.title: How a livery is built from parts
articles.summary: A paint scheme is a base colour, one or two accents and a trim colour, laid on the car's named parts. Work part by part, not with boxes across the sheet.
articles.what: The car lies flat on the sheet: two side panels, hood, roof, trunk, front and rear bumper and spoiler. On a side panel, height is measured from the roof-line down to the rocker. 0.00 to 0.12 is the window edge; 0.10 to 0.25 the beltline, where a thin stripe separates body from glass; 0.30 to 0.65 the door centre where the number lives, so keep it calm; 0.64 to 0.70 a pinstripe above the lower band; 0.68 to 1.00 the lower body and rocker band, the classic place for the second colour. The front 22 percent of the length is the front fender and the rear 24 percent the rear quarter. Sides mirror each other, so one region can take both.
when: You are planning a livery from scratch.
You are not sure where on the sheet a stripe should go.
how: Decide the base colour, one accent and a trim colour.
Place each by named part (left side, hood, roof), then by a band within it.
Keep the door centre calm for the number.
Put the second colour in the lower band, and mirror to the other side.
Check the preview and fix anything off.
tips: The built-in design recipes already know these proportions; use them for any scheme or throwback.
pitfalls: The outside assistants refuse very large boxes; name the part instead.

articles.title: Classic scheme families and era palettes
articles.summary: Retro lower band, classic twin stripes, two-tone, colour block, bookends and stealth are the common families. Each era has its own palette of colours.
articles.what: Retro lower band: body colour, a bold lower band, a thin trim line above it, bumpers and spoiler in the band colour (Pepsi-style, Sunoco-style, Gulf-style). Classic twin stripes: two parallel stripes along the sides continuing as a centre stripe over hood, roof and trunk. Two-tone: second colour from the belt down plus hood and bumpers. Colour block: hood, roof and rear quarters in different colours. Bookends: contrasting front and rear ends with a quiet body. Stealth: dark on dark with one thin accent. Eras: 1960s to 70s powder blue and orange, navy and white, harvest orange, rust brown, mustard; 1970s to 80s red, white and blue with chrome trim, black and gold, blue and yellow; 1980s hot pink, cyan and purple on black or white; 1990s teal, purple and magenta splashes; modern is matte black with one accent, or white with one strong colour.

You need a palette for an era.

Lay the colours on the parts as in the parts article.

pitfalls: More than one twist makes the scheme look busy.

articles.title: What makes a scheme look professional
articles.summary: Use one dominant colour (about 60 percent), one accent (about 30) and one trim (about 10). Keep the number calm, line the blocks up across the car and never paint over numbers or sponsors.
articles.what: White or black as the quiet colour lets the accents sing. The side band continues the bumper colour, and the hood stripe continues over the roof and trunk. Keep contrast between the number and its background, and do not run a busy stripe behind the numbers. Matte paint with chrome trim lines is the modern retro look; gloss everywhere is the showroom look. Finish choices: matte for flat paint, gloss for showroom, satin in between, chrome for trim lines (a chrome pinstripe on a matte car reads as real chrome), and metallic or candy blocks beside flat blocks create the pop through opposite colour and opposite shine.

articles.title: Exact brand colours, Pantone and colour-blind friendly schemes
articles.summary: Type an exact hex colour into the zone's BASE COLOR box, or sample one with the eyedropper. Shokker has no Pantone library and no colour-blind preview, so convert a Pantone colour to hex first; strong light-dark contrast is the general way to keep a scheme readable.
articles.what: Every zone's BASE COLOR has a colour swatch and a text box that takes a hex value like #1a6dff, so a brand colour can be entered exactly. Pick Color (P) samples a colour from the paint, and the eyedropper button next to BASE COLOR can pick one from anywhere on screen. Shokker does not include a Pantone book: look up the Pantone colour's hex value elsewhere and type it in. iRacing lights the car with sun, shadow and the metal in the spec map, so the same hex can look different on track. There is no colour-blind simulation or colour-blind mode in Shokker, and the app's docs say nothing specific about colour blindness. The app's own readability advice is to separate colours and numbers by value (light against dark); as general design practice, that also helps colour-blind viewers.
when: A sponsor gives you an exact brand colour.
Your team colours must match across several cars.
You want a scheme that reads clearly for colour-blind drivers.
how: 1. Open the zone and set BASE COLOR to Use solid color.
2. Click the hex box next to the swatch, type the value (for example #1a6dff) and press Enter.
3. To copy a colour that is already on the paint, use Pick Color (P) and click it.
4. For a Pantone colour, look up its hex value first, then type it in.
5. Render and check in iRacing; adjust brightness slightly if metal or lighting shifts it.
tips: Write your team's hex values down and reuse them on every car you paint so the set matches.
pitfalls: Metallic and chrome finishes multiply your colour by the metal in the spec, so a brand colour can read darker; use a non-metal finish when the colour must be exact.
Typing a hex in the zone's colour-match picker chooses which pixels to catch; it does not recolour them. Use BASE COLOR to set a colour.

deep.heading: Exact colour versus what iRacing shows
deep.body: The hex you type is exactly what goes into the paint file. iRacing then lights it: sun, shadow and reflections change how bright it looks, and the metal value in the spec map multiplies it, so metallic and chrome areas look darker than the flat colour. For a colour that must match a logo, use a gloss or satin finish with little metal, and compare on track rather than in the preview.

deep.heading: Colours that read for everyone
deep.body: The readability rule Shokker's helper follows is contrast: put a colour next to a clearly lighter or darker one, and make numbers and sponsors light on dark or dark on light. Shokker has no colour-blind check, so this is general design practice rather than an app feature: schemes that rely only on hue, such as red next to green at the same brightness, are the ones colour-blind viewers commonly cannot separate, and the same light-dark rule helps there.

faq.q: Can I match a Pantone colour?
faq.a: There is no Pantone library. Convert the Pantone colour to hex and type it into BASE COLOR.

faq.q: How do I enter an exact colour?
faq.a: Type the hex value into the box next to the BASE COLOR swatch.

faq.q: Is there a colour-blind mode?
faq.a: No, Shokker has no colour-blind mode or preview. Building the scheme on light-dark contrast is general good practice.

mistakes.cause: A metallic or chrome finish multiplies the colour by the metal value.
mistakes.fix: Use a finish with little metal for colour-critical areas.

mistakes.symptom: Typing the hex did not change the colour.
mistakes.cause: It was typed into the colour-match picker, which only chooses pixels.
mistakes.fix: Type it into BASE COLOR's hex box instead.

protips: Keep a note of your team's hex values and reuse them on every car you paint (Shokker paints cars only in this build, not helmets or suits).
